b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks: An independent clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence (1 mark).

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text: Describe two effects a semicolon can create in creative writing.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
1 marks for each effect, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• It can create contrast/juxtaposition by placing two opposing ideas side by side (1)
• It can extend a description by adding a second layer of detail (1)
• It can build tension or suspense by linking stillness with action (1)
• It can control pace by creating a pause shorter than a full stop (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text: Explain why the following sentence uses the semicolon incorrectly: 'He ran through the forest; gasping for air.' Write a corrected version.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Identifies that 'gasping for air' is not a complete/independent clause (1)
• Explains that both sides of a semicolon must be able to stand alone as sentences (1)
• Explains that 'gasping for air' is a fragment/phrase without a subject and main verb (1)
• Provides a correct version, e.g. 'He ran through the forest; his lungs burned with every breath' (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text: Explain how a writer could use semicolons alongside other sentence structures (such as short sentences) to create a varied and effective piece of descriptive writing. Use examples in your answer.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
Award up to 6 marks across these areas:
• Explains that short sentences create sharp, punchy effects such as tension or shock (1)
• Explains that semicolons create longer, flowing sentences that can develop or contrast ideas (1)
• Explains that varying between short and semicolon-linked sentences shows control of pace (1)
• Provides an effective example of a short sentence used for impact (1)
• Provides an effective example of a semicolon sentence used for contrast, description, or suspense (1)
• Links this variation to the AO6 requirement for a range of sentence structures and punctuation (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text:
Read the following extract from a student's creative writing:

'The house stood at the end of the lane. It was old. The windows were dark. The garden was overgrown. Nobody had lived there for years.'

Evaluate this extract and rewrite it to include at least one semicolon, explaining how your changes improve the writing.
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
Award marks across two areas:

Evaluation of the original (up to 4 marks):
• Identifies that the original uses only simple/short sentences with full stops (1)
• Comments that this creates a repetitive, monotonous rhythm (1)
• Notes the lack of punctuation range limits the technical accuracy mark (1)
• Recognises that while short sentences can create tension, using only short sentences loses impact (1)

Rewrite and explanation (up to 5 marks):
• Rewrites with at least one correctly used semicolon (both halves are independent clauses) (1)
• Explains the effect of the semicolon (e.g. contrast, extension, tension) (1)
• Shows variation in sentence structure beyond just the semicolon (1)
• Explains how the rewrite demonstrates a wider range of punctuation for AO6 (1)
• Quality and sophistication of the rewritten passage (1)

b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.text:
Write a description suggested by the following image: a narrow street at night, lit by a single lamp.

In your writing, you must use at least two semicolons correctly and demonstrate a range of punctuation.

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)
b3e9f051-a4d9-4d22-ad48-2b26fb29f855.marks:
AO5 Content and Organisation (24 marks) — assessed using AQA Level 1–4 descriptors:
• Top band (19–24) Compelling, convincing communication. Varied and inventive structural features. Extensive vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices.
• Upper-mid band (13–18) Consistently clear communication. Effective structural features. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect.
• Lower-mid band (7–12) Some successful communication. Some use of structural features. Conscious use of vocabulary.
• Lower band (1–6) Simple, limited communication. Simple vocabulary and structural features.

AO6 Technical Accuracy (16 marks) — assessed using AQA Level 1–4 descriptors:
• Top band (13–16) Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms. Secure control of complex grammar. High accuracy in spelling.
• Upper-mid band (9–12) Range of punctuation mostly used with success. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
• Lower-mid band (5–8) Some control of punctuation. Attempts variety of sentence forms. Some accurate spelling.
• Lower band (1–4) Some evidence of conscious punctuation. Simple sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

For this question, look specifically for:
• At least two correctly used semicolons (both halves must be independent clauses)
• Semicolons used for deliberate effect (contrast, extension, or tension)
• Range of other punctuation (commas, colons, dashes, ellipses, exclamation marks)
• Variation in sentence length and structure

9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.text: “Cars are convenient, comfortable and save time. However, we need to use them less.” Write a speech to your local council arguing your point of view on this statement.
9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.marks:
AO5 (24 marks): Top band (19–24) Convincing and compelling. Tone assuredly matched. Extensive vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices. Varied structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs.

Upper-mid band (13–18) Consistently clear. Tone consistently matched. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary. Effective use of structural features.

Lower-mid band (7–12) Some success. Some matching of tone. Varied vocabulary. Some structural features.

Lower band (1–6) Simple. Simple awareness. Simple vocabulary.

9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.text: Write the opening paragraph of a speech arguing that schools should start later in the morning.
9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.marks: Should include: hook (rhetorical question, striking fact, or bold statement), clear thesis, appropriate register for audience. Top band: convincing opening with deliberate crafting. Upper-mid band: clear opening with some devices.

9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.text: Explain the five-part structure for an argumentative response and why each part matters.
9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.marks: 1. Opening (hook + thesis). 2–4. Three body paragraphs (point, evidence, explanation, crafted language). 5. Counter-argument + conclusion. Each part serves the argument. Top band: explains how the structure creates “fluid sequencing.”

9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.text: What are discourse markers? Explain the difference between Level 2 and Level 4 use of discourse markers.
9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.marks: Discourse markers connect ideas between paragraphs. Lower-mid band: “some use” — mechanical (Firstly, Secondly). Top band: “seamlessly integrated” — woven naturally into sentences. Examples of each.

9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.text: Write a paragraph that uses at least two rhetorical devices to argue that public transport should be free for under-18s.
9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.marks: Should include deliberate use of devices (e.g. rhetorical question + direct address, or tricolon + emotive language). Top band: devices serve the argument. Lower-mid band: devices used randomly.

9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.text: Explain why the AQA mark scheme caps AO5 at Level 2 if you do not address the focus of the task.
9a78b2e8-360d-4848-acf7-6590a4139ab6.marks: Mark scheme states communication cannot be “clear or convincing” if it doesn’t address the task. Maximum 12 out of 24 marks. Every paragraph must link back to the statement. 2 marks for citing the rule, 2 marks for explaining its impact.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks: A word that imitates the natural sound of the thing it describes (1 mark). Accept examples such as 'crash,' 'hiss,' 'buzz' if accompanied by a brief definition.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text: Describe two ways a writer could use the sense of sound to create atmosphere in a descriptive piece.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks: One mark for each way described, up to 2 marks. For example: • Use onomatopoeia such as 'crash' or 'hiss' to make the reader hear the sound directly (1 mark). • Use a contrast between silence and sudden noise to create tension or surprise (1 mark). • Use repetition of sounds (e.g. 'yip yip yip') to convey a relentless or overwhelming atmosphere (1 mark). Accept any two valid methods with brief explanation.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text: Explain how the 'zooming in' technique can help a student organise a descriptive writing response effectively.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks: Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation that covers: • Definition: zooming in means moving from a wide overview of a scene to a small, specific detail (1 mark). • Effect on reader: it mimics how the human eye works, creating a sense of discovery as focus narrows (1 mark). • Structural benefit: it provides a logical, deliberate organisation rather than random listing of details (1 mark). • Link to assessment: strong answers show 'varied and inventive use of structural features' at the highest band for content and organisation (1 mark). Accept reverse zoom (close to wide) if clearly explained.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text: Explain how Peter Fleming uses personification to describe the train crash in Source A. Use specific examples from the text to support your answer.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks:
Award up to 6 marks across two levels:
Upper band (4-6): Clear, detailed explanation with specific examples and analysis of effect. For example:
• The train 'sprawled foolishly' — the adverb 'foolishly' gives the train a human quality of embarrassment or stupidity, creating dark humour from the wreckage (up to 2 marks).
• The carriages are 'disposed in attitudes' and the last one remains 'primly, on the rails' — 'primly' suggests prim, proper behaviour, as if the carriage is morally superior to the others, adding absurdist comedy (up to 2 marks).
• The engine has 'a defiant and naughty look' and is 'definitely conscious of indiscretion' — it is presented as a mischievous child who knows it has done wrong, which undercuts the danger of the crash with comic tone (up to 2 marks).
Lower band (1-3): Some relevant examples identified with simple or partial explanation of effect.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text:
Read the following student response to a descriptive writing task:

'The beach was nice. The sea was blue and the sand was golden. There were some seagulls flying around. The sun was warm and it felt relaxing. I could hear the waves.'

Evaluate this response against the Level 4 descriptors for content and organisation. To what extent does it meet the standard? What specific improvements would you recommend?
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks:
Award up to 9 marks using a three-level structure:
Top band (7-9): Perceptive evaluation that identifies specific weaknesses and offers detailed, practical improvements. The response should note:
• The writing tells rather than shows — 'The beach was nice' is a statement, not a description. Level 4 requires 'convincing and compelling' communication.
• Vocabulary is generic ('nice,' 'blue,' 'golden,' 'warm') — Level 4 requires 'extensive and ambitious vocabulary.'
• Only two senses are used (sight and touch/hearing briefly) and none are developed with figurative language.
• No structural variety — every sentence follows the same subject-verb-complement pattern.
• Improvements: use specific sensory detail ('the gritty warmth of sand between my toes'), figurative language ('waves exhaling against the shore'), varied sentence forms, and a deliberate structure (e.g. zooming in).
Mid band (4-6): Clear identification of some weaknesses with some useful suggestions.
Lower band (1-3): Simple or limited comments, may identify it as 'not very good' without specific analysis.

65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.text:
You are going to enter a creative writing competition. Your entry will be judged by a panel of English teachers.

Write a description suggested by this task: 'Describe a place where everything has stopped.'

(24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy)

Plan and write your response. You should aim to use precise sensory detail, varied sentence structures, and at least one example of the 'zooming in' technique.
65fece77-1755-4524-aec4-f656561e3dbe.marks:
Content and Organisation (24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Communication is convincing and compelling. Tone, style and register assuredly matched to purpose. Extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices. Varied and inventive structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Communication is consistently clear. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect. Effective structural features. Coherent paragraphs with integrated discourse markers.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success. Conscious use of vocabulary. Some structural features. Some use of paragraphs.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication. Simple vocabulary. Limited structural features.

Technical Accuracy (16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms for effect. High-level spelling including ambitious vocabulary.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation range. Attempts variety of sentence forms.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Simple sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

Indicative content: Students should demonstrate careful observation of a still or frozen scene using multiple senses. Strong responses will use zooming in/out, figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification), varied sentence lengths for pace control, and ambitious vocabulary. The 'stopped' prompt lends itself to contrasts between stillness and implied movement, silence and implied sound.

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks: A simile is a figure of speech that compares two different things using 'like' or 'as' (1 mark).

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text: Describe two ways a writer can make a simile effective in creative writing.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
1 marks for each valid way, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• By making the comparison unexpected or original, so it creates a vivid image (1)
• By matching the simile to the mood or atmosphere of the piece (1)
• By using the simile to reveal something about the character or narrator’s feelings (1)
• By extending the comparison across several sentences to create a sustained effect (1)

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text: Explain why using clichéd similes (such as 'cold as ice' or 'quiet as a mouse') is likely to lower a student's mark in Paper 1 Section B.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation. Possible points:
• Clichés are overused expressions that have lost their impact — they do not create a vivid or original image in the reader’s mind (1)
• The mark scheme rewards ‘ambitious vocabulary’ and ‘crafting of linguistic devices’ — clichés demonstrate neither (1)
• Clichés suggest the writer is not thinking carefully about their word choices, which signals Level 1 or 2 writing (1)
• They fail to convey a specific mood or perspective because they are so generic (1)
• Examiners read thousands of responses — original language stands out, clichés do not (1)

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text: Explain how an extended metaphor can help a student achieve Level 4 in the AQA Paper 1 creative writing task. You should refer to specific features of the Level 4 mark scheme descriptors in your answer.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Award up to 6 marks. Possible points:
• Level 4 requires ‘sustained crafting of linguistic devices’ — an extended metaphor that runs across a paragraph or whole response demonstrates sustained, deliberate crafting (1–2)
• Level 4 requires ‘extensive and ambitious vocabulary’ — an extended metaphor naturally generates a semantic field of related vocabulary, showing range and ambition (1–2)
• Level 4 requires ‘compelling, convincing communication’ — a well-developed extended metaphor creates a strong, immersive atmosphere that draws the reader in (1–2)
• Reference to how structure supports the device: an extended metaphor can unify a paragraph and give it coherence, linking to ‘varied and inventive use of structural features’ (1)
• Example: comparing a storm to an argument across multiple sentences (thunder as shouting, lightning as accusations, silence as a truce) shows control and ambition (1)

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text:
Read the following student's opening paragraph:

'The forest was dark. The trees were tall. The wind blew through the branches like a cold breeze. It was scary. I walked slowly.'

Evaluate this paragraph's use of figurative language and suggest how it could be improved to reach Level 3 or above.
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Award up to 9 marks using a best-fit approach.
Top band (7-9): Clear, detailed evaluation. Identifies that the simile ‘like a cold breeze’ is weak because wind already IS a breeze, so no real comparison is being made. Notes the reliance on simple adjectives (‘dark’, ‘tall’, ‘scary’) with no figurative language to create atmosphere. Offers specific, practical improvements, e.g. replacing ‘like a cold breeze’ with an original simile (‘the wind moved through the branches like fingers searching for something lost’), using personification for the trees, or adding a metaphor that conveys the narrator’s fear.
Mid band (4-6): Some valid points about the weakness of the simile and the lack of vivid language. Suggestions for improvement are general rather than specific.
Lower band (1-3): Simple identification that the writing is ‘boring’ or ‘needs more description’ without explaining why or offering concrete alternatives.

70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.text:
You are going to enter a creative writing competition. Your entry will be judged by a panel of experienced writers.

Write a description suggested by this picture: a lone figure standing at the edge of a cliff, looking out over a stormy sea.

You should use figurative language, including at least one original simile and one example of personification, to create a vivid atmosphere.

(24 marks for content and organisation
16 marks for technical accuracy)
70facceb-ef6a-4607-a9f8-421f7d55a387.marks:
Content and Organisation (AO5, 24 marks):
Top band (19–24) Communication is convincing and compelling. Tone, style and register assuredly matched to purpose. Extensive and ambitious vocabulary with sustained crafting of linguistic devices (simile, personification, metaphor). Varied and inventive structural features. Fluently linked paragraphs.
Upper-mid band (13–18) Communication is consistently clear. Increasingly sophisticated vocabulary chosen for effect with a range of successful linguistic devices. Effective use of structural features. Coherent paragraphs with integrated discourse markers.
Lower-mid band (7–12) Communicates with some success. Conscious use of vocabulary with some use of linguistic devices. Some use of structural features and paragraphs.
Lower band (1–6) Simple communication. Simple vocabulary and simple linguistic devices. Random paragraph structure.

Technical Accuracy (AO6, 16 marks):
Top band (13–16) Consistently secure sentence demarcation. Wide range of punctuation with high accuracy. Full range of sentence forms. High level of spelling accuracy.
Upper-mid band (9–12) Mostly secure demarcation. Range of punctuation mostly successful. Variety of sentence forms. Generally accurate spelling.
Lower-mid band (5–8) Mostly secure demarcation, sometimes accurate. Some control of punctuation. Attempts variety of sentence forms.
Lower band (1–4) Occasional sentence demarcation. Simple range of sentence forms. Accurate basic spelling.

826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.text:
For this question focus on the second part of the source, from line 20 to the end.

In this part of the source, the hyena could be seen as funny or threatening.

To what extent do you agree or disagree with this statement?

In your response, you could:
• consider your impressions of how the hyena behaves
• comment on the methods the writer uses to present the hyena as funny or threatening
• support your response with references to the text.
826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.marks:
Top band (16-20): Shows perceptive and detailed evaluation. Evaluates critically and in detail the effect(s) on the reader. Shows perceptive understanding of the writer's methods. Selects a range of judicious textual detail. Develops a convincing and critical response to the focus of the question.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Shows clear and relevant evaluation. Evaluates clearly the effect(s) on the reader. Shows clear understanding of writer's methods. Selects a range of relevant textual references. Makes a clear and relevant response to the focus of the question.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Shows some attempts at evaluation. Makes some evaluative comment(s) on effect(s) on the reader. Shows some understanding of writer's methods. Selects some appropriate textual reference(s). Makes some response to the focus of the question.
Lower band (1-5): Shows simple, limited evaluation. Makes simple, limited evaluative comment(s). Shows simple, limited understanding of writer's methods. Selects simple, limited textual reference(s). Makes a simple, limited response.
Students may discuss: onomatopoeia of 'yip yip yip' creating comedy; metaphor of 'indoor track' making the hyena seem absurd; 'I prepared for my end' conveying genuine terror; the anti-climactic vomiting scene; 'maniacal beast' suggesting real danger; juxtaposition of humour and threat throughout.

826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.text:
A student said: 'In this part of the text, the writer makes the reader feel increasingly anxious about what will happen to Pi.'

To what extent do you agree?

In your response, you could:
• consider Pi's thoughts and feelings
• comment on the methods the writer uses to create a sense of anxiety
• support your response with references to the text.

(Focus on the source from line 20 to the end.)
826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.marks:
Top band (16-20): Perceptive, detailed evaluation with judicious textual detail. Develops a convincing and critical response. Analyses writer's methods perceptively.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear, relevant evaluation. Explains effects clearly with relevant references. Makes a clear response to the focus.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some evaluative comment with some appropriate references. Attempts to respond to the statement.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited evaluation with basic references.
Students may include:
• 'I was seized by fear and could only watch' – passive construction suggests helplessness
• 'Each time it came from the stern I tensed' – first person physical reaction conveys visceral fear
• 'I prepared for my end' – blunt, fatalistic short sentence increases anxiety
• The repetitive circling creates suspense through unpredictability
• Counter-argument: the anti-climax of the vomiting releases anxiety, suggesting the writer does not sustain it throughout.

826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.text:
Read again the first part of the source, from lines 1 to 9.

Answer all parts of this question.

Tick one box for each question.

a) What worries Pi about the hyena?
b) How do hyenas usually attack?
c) What sort of attackers are hyenas?
d) What does Pi hope will distract the hyena away from him?
826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.marks:
a) Remembering what his father told him about hyenas [1 mark]
b) As a group [1 mark]
c) Tough [1 mark]
d) The other animals on the boat [1 mark]

Total: 4 marks (1 per correct answer)

826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.text:
Look in detail at this extract, from lines 10 to 19 of the source.

How does the writer use language here to describe the hyena's appearance?

You could include the writer's choice of:
• words and phrases
• language features and techniques
• sentence forms.
826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive, detailed analysis. Analyses the effects of the writer's choices of language. Selects a range of judicious textual detail. Makes sophisticated and accurate use of subject terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear, relevant explanation. Explains clearly the effects of language choices. Selects a range of relevant textual detail. Makes clear and accurate use of subject terminology.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding and comment. Attempts to comment on the effect of language. Selects some appropriate textual detail.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, limited comment. Offers simple comment on the effect of language.
Students may discuss: adjectives 'ugly', 'shaggy', 'coarse'; verbs 'bungled'; contrast with 'classy ostentation of a leopard's'; simile 'like the symptoms of a skin disease'; adverbs 'too massive', 'ridiculously'; humour/hyperbole 'suffering from a receding hairline'; short declarative sentences; antithesis 'doglike, but like no dog anyone would want as a pet'.

826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.text:
A student said: 'The writer makes the hyena seem more pathetic than dangerous by the end of the extract.'

To what extent do you agree?

In your response, you could:
• consider your impressions of the hyena at the end of the extract
• comment on the methods the writer uses to present the hyena
• support your response with references to the text.

(Focus on the source from line 40 to the end.)
826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.marks:
Top band (16-20): Perceptive, detailed evaluation. Analyses writer's methods with judicious references. Develops convincing critical response.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Clear, relevant evaluation with relevant textual detail.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Some evaluative comments with some appropriate references.
Lower band (1-5): Simple, limited evaluation.
Students may include:
• 'It hacked and coughed' – verbs suggest vulnerability and sickness rather than aggression
• 'Abruptly it vomited' – the blunt short sentence creates bathos/anti-climax
• 'exploring the furthest confines of animal anguish' – hyperbolic phrase shifts the reader's response towards sympathy
• 'shaking and whining and turning around on itself' – tricolon of weak, distressed actions
• Counter-argument: earlier in the extract the hyena is described as a 'maniacal beast', suggesting genuine danger that lingers even after the anti-climax.

826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.text:
You now need to think about the structure of the source as a whole.

The text is from the middle of a novel.

How has the writer structured the text to create tension?

You could write about:
• how tension has increased or decreased by the end of the source
• how the writer uses structure to create an effect
• the writer's use of any other structural features, such as changes in mood, tone or perspective.
826f70e2-88a3-4c45-ad0b-9267920d289c.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive, detailed analysis of structural features. Analyses effects with judicious examples. Sophisticated use of subject terminology.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear, relevant explanation of structural features. Selects relevant examples. Clear use of subject terminology.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some understanding and comment on structural features.
Lower band (1-2): Simple, limited comment on structure.
Students may discuss: exposition about hyenas foreshadowing danger; pivotal point when hyena appears; rising action as erratic behaviour escalates; first person perspective sharing Pi's terror; juxtaposition of vicious nature and vulnerable ending; anti-climactic conclusion releasing tension; repetition of circling creating cyclical structure; shifts between action and description.

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
1 mark(s) for a clear definition, e.g.:
• Language that appeals to one or more of the five senses (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) to help the reader experience a scene.

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.text: Describe two ways a writer could use 'show don't tell' to convey a character's fear.
d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.marks:
1 marks for each valid way, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• Describe physical reactions such as trembling hands, shallow breathing, a racing heart or cold sweat (1 mark)
• Describe the character's actions, such as backing away, freezing, or gripping something tightly (1 mark)
• Use sensory details that create a threatening atmosphere, such as sounds, shadows, or cold air (1 mark)
• Use a powerful verb that implies fear without naming it, e.g. 'stumbled' or 'recoiled' (1 mark)

d96fa366-519f-4c25-b09e-3ccb72b0676c.text: Explain how Peter Fleming uses the verb 'cannonaded' to describe the impact of the suitcase during the train crash in Source A (Paper 2, 2026 sample). You should comment on the effect this has on the reader.

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.text: Explain how a writer could use logos to argue that public transport should be made cheaper.
9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Clear explanation of how logos works with specific examples. E.g.: A writer could use logos by including a statistic such as 'for every £1 invested in buses, the local economy gains £4' to provide concrete evidence that the policy makes financial sense. They could also use cause-and-effect reasoning: 'if fares are reduced, more people will use buses, reducing traffic congestion and lowering road maintenance costs.' This logical chain shows the audience that the argument is rational, not just emotional.
Lower band (1-2): Simple or general explanation. E.g.: They could use facts and statistics to prove their point, like saying how much money it would save.

9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.text: Explain why using all three rhetorical appeals (ethos, logos, pathos) together is more effective than relying on just one.
9cea9234-9798-4fae-9700-4b759b353743.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed explanation showing understanding of how the appeals complement each other, with examples. E.g.: Using all three appeals creates a more convincing and well-rounded argument. Logos provides the evidence that satisfies a sceptical reader's need for proof, while pathos engages the reader's emotions and makes them care about the issue on a personal level. Ethos underpins both by ensuring the reader trusts the writer enough to accept the evidence and respond to the emotional appeal. A response that relies only on pathos risks seeming manipulative, while one that uses only logos may feel cold and fail to motivate the reader to act.
Mid band (3-4): Some valid explanation but may lack examples or detail. E.g.: Using all three together makes the argument stronger because logos convinces the reader's brain, pathos convinces their heart, and ethos makes them trust the writer. If you only use emotion, the reader might not believe you.
Lower band (1-2): Simple awareness. E.g.: It is better to use all three because it makes your writing more persuasive and gets more marks.

• Counter-argument: the anti-climax of the vomiting releases anxiety, suggesting the writer does not sustain it throughout.

2b68cb12-f77a-4045-a815-6dfe9c594ebb.text: Describe two ways a writer can make a simile effective in creative writing.
2b68cb12-f77a-4045-a815-6dfe9c594ebb.marks:

• By extending the comparison across several sentences to create a sustained effect (1)

2b68cb12-f77a-4045-a815-6dfe9c594ebb.text: Explain why using clichéd similes (such as 'cold as ice' or 'quiet as a mouse') is likely to lower a student's mark in Paper 1 Section B.
2b68cb12-f77a-4045-a815-6dfe9c594ebb.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation. Possible points:
• Clichés are overused expressions that have lost their impact — they do not create a vivid or original image in the reader’s mind (1)
• The mark scheme rewards ‘ambitious vocabulary’ and ‘crafting of linguistic devices’ — clichés demonstrate neither (1)
• Clichés suggest the writer is not thinking carefully about their word choices, which signals Level 1 or 2 writing (1)
• They fail to convey a specific mood or perspective because they are so generic (1)
• Examiners read thousands of responses — original language stands out, clichés do not (1)

2b68cb12-f77a-4045-a815-6dfe9c594ebb.text: Explain how an extended metaphor can help a student achieve Level 4 in the AQA Paper 1 creative writing task. You should refer to specific features of the Level 4 mark scheme descriptors in your answer.

• Level 4 requires ‘sustained crafting of linguistic devices’ — an extended metaphor that runs across a paragraph or whole response demonstrates sustained, deliberate crafting (1–2)
• Level 4 requires ‘extensive and ambitious vocabulary’ — an extended metaphor naturally generates a semantic field of related vocabulary, showing range and ambition (1–2)
• Level 4 requires ‘compelling, convincing communication’ — a well-developed extended metaphor creates a strong, immersive atmosphere that draws the reader in (1–2)
• Reference to how structure supports the device: an extended metaphor can unify a paragraph and give it coherence, linking to ‘varied and inventive use of structural features’ (1)
• Example: comparing a storm to an argument across multiple sentences (thunder as shouting, lightning as accusations, silence as a truce) shows control and ambition (1)

Evaluate this paragraph's use of figurative language and suggest how it could be improved to reach Level 3 or above.

Offers specific, practical improvements, e.g. replacing ‘like a cold breeze’ with an original simile (‘the wind moved through the branches like fingers searching for something lost’), using personification for the trees, or adding a metaphor that conveys the narrator’s fear.
Mid band (4-6): Some valid points about the weakness of the simile and the lack of vivid language. Suggestions for improvement are general rather than specific.
Lower band (1-3): Simple identification that the writing is ‘boring’ or ‘needs more description’ without explaining why or offering concrete alternatives.

Read the following paragraph written by a student:

Identify four technical accuracy errors in this paragraph and correct each one.
68e41b2f-7a1c-46ea-a900-3d5e1f656816.marks:
1 mark(s) for correctly identifying and correcting any four of the following:
• Comma splice after 'planet' — should be a full stop, semicolon, or conjunction
• 'loads of' — informal; should be 'significant' or similar
• Double negative 'no one does nothing' — should be 'no one does anything'
• 'goverment' — misspelled; should be 'government'
• 'its' — should be 'it's' (contraction of 'it is')
• 'dont' — should be 'don't' (missing apostrophe)

68e41b2f-7a1c-46ea-a900-3d5e1f656816.text: Describe two differences between Level 2 and Level 4 in the AO6 technical accuracy mark scheme.
68e41b2f-7a1c-46ea-a900-3d5e1f656816.marks:
1 marks for each valid difference, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• Level 2 requires 'some control of a range of punctuation' whereas Level 4 requires a 'wide range of punctuation used with a high level of accuracy' (1 mark)
• Level 2 requires 'varied use of vocabulary' whereas Level 4 requires 'extensive and ambitious use of vocabulary' (1 mark)
• Level 2 says sentence demarcation is 'sometimes accurate' whereas Level 4 says it is 'consistently accurate' (1 mark)
• Level 2 says 'attempts a variety of sentence forms' whereas Level 4 says 'uses a full range of appropriate sentence forms for effect' (1 mark)

68e41b2f-7a1c-46ea-a900-3d5e1f656816.text: Explain why varying sentence forms is important for achieving a high mark in AO6 on Paper 2 Question 5.
68e41b2f-7a1c-46ea-a900-3d5e1f656816.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a clear explanation that may include:
• The AO6 mark scheme at Level 4 requires 'a full range of appropriate sentence forms for effect' — not just variety but deliberate choices (1 mark)
• Simple sentences can be used for emphasis or dramatic impact, e.g. 'This must change.' (1 mark)
• Complex sentences with subordinate clauses allow development of ideas, cause and effect, and show grammatical control (1 mark)
• Varying sentence openers (adverbial, prepositional, participial, conditional) demonstrates range and confidence to the examiner (1 mark)
• The key word is 'for effect' — the examiner needs to see that sentence choices are purposeful, not random (1 mark)

68e41b2f-7a1c-46ea-a900-3d5e1f656816.text: Explain how a student could improve their punctuation from Level 2 ('some control of a range of punctuation') to Level 4 ('wide range of punctuation used with a high level of accuracy').
68e41b2f-7a1c-46ea-a900-3d5e1f656816.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a detailed explanation that may include:
• At Level 2, students typically rely on full stops, commas and capital letters — Level 4 requires going beyond these basics (1 mark)
• Using semicolons correctly to join two closely related independent clauses (1 mark)
• Using colons to introduce explanations, lists or elaborations (1 mark)
• Using dashes for parenthetical information or dramatic emphasis (1 mark)
• Avoiding common errors such as comma splicing, missing apostrophes in possession, and overusing exclamation marks (1 mark)
• The mark scheme stresses 'high level of accuracy' — punctuation must be correct, not just present; one well-placed semicolon is better than five misused ones (1 mark)
• Using punctuation to support the form and purpose — e.g. rhetorical questions in a speech (1 mark)
